questiontext.text: What does bubble sort do on each pass through the array?

answer.text: Repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are out of order

feedback.text: Correct — adjacent comparisons let the largest remaining element "bubble" to the end.

answer.text: Selects the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it to the front

feedback.text: That describes selection sort.

answer.text: Partitions the array around a pivot element

feedback.text: That describes quicksort.

answer.text: Merges two sorted halves into one sorted array

feedback.text: That describes merge sort.

generalfeedback.text: Bubble sort walks the array comparing neighbours and swapping out-of-order pairs; each pass pushes the next largest element into place at the end.

generalfeedback.text: In the worst case (e.g. a reverse-sorted array) bubble sort performs on the order of n^2 comparisons and swaps.

questiontext.text: With the early-exit optimization, what is bubble sort's best-case time complexity on an already-sorted array?

feedback.text: Correct — one clean pass with no swaps lets the algorithm stop early.
Without early-exit it would be O(n^2), but the optimization detects the sorted array in one pass.

generalfeedback.text: An early-exit flag lets bubble sort stop after a single swap-free pass, making it O(n) and adaptive on nearly-sorted input.

questiontext.text: Which statements about bubble sort are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Each pass moves the largest unsorted element to its final position at the end

feedback.text: Yes — that is why it is called "bubbling up".

answer.text: With an early-exit flag it becomes adaptive on nearly-sorted data

feedback.text: Yes — it can finish in O(n) when few swaps are needed.

answer.text: It has average-case time complexity O(n log n)

feedback.text: No — the average case is O(n^2).

answer.text: It requires an auxiliary array proportional to n

feedback.text: No — bubble sort is in-place, O(1) extra space.

generalfeedback.text: Bubble sort: bubbles the max to the end each pass, is stable and in-place, is adaptive with early-exit, but is O(n^2) on average.

questiontext.text: Which is the most reasonable use of bubble sort?

answer.text: Teaching sorting concepts, or sorting very small or nearly-sorted inputs where simplicity matters

feedback.text: Correct — its clarity and early-exit make it fine for tiny or almost-sorted data, but not for large arrays.

answer.text: Sorting millions of records in a production database

feedback.text: No — O(n^2) is far too slow at that scale; use an O(n log n) sort.

answer.text: When you must guarantee O(n log n) worst-case performance

feedback.text: No — bubble sort's worst case is O(n^2).

generalfeedback.text: Bubble sort is mainly pedagogical; in practice it only suits tiny or nearly-sorted inputs where its simplicity and early-exit pay off.
